Newark.metaTitle: Newark, NJ Sewer Lateral Rules & CIPP Lining
Newark.metaDescription: Newark makes owners pay for the building sewer past the curb, requires a licensed master plumber and a bond, and runs 17 CSO outfalls. See the rules and where CIPP fits.
Newark.article:
Newark's Combined Sewers Run Under an Airport and a River

Newark's local sewers are owned and run by the City of Newark's Department of Water and Sewer Utilities, while the wastewater is treated regionally by the Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission. Much of the city — roughly eleven square miles of it — is served by a combined sewer system that carries sewage and stormwater in the same pipes, and in heavy rain that system overflows through 17 permitted outfalls: a dozen along the Passaic River and five more around the peripheral ditch that rings Newark Liberty International Airport. The city runs eleven netting and screening facilities to catch floatables before they discharge. That combined-sewer reality is the backdrop to every private lateral repair in the city.

Who Pays for the Building Sewer Past the Curb

Newark's code, Title 32, draws the line at the curb. The portion of the building sewer beyond the curbline is built and repaired by the city's Division of Sewers and Water Supply, but the code is explicit that this is done at the expense of the owner. In practice the lateral serving your building is your financial responsibility — the city may control the work in the street, but the bill for it lands on the property owner. Knowing that split in advance is what lets an owner plan a repair rather than be surprised by an assessment after an emergency dig.

A Licensed Master Plumber, a Permit, and a Bond

Newark does not allow casual sewer work. Under Title 32, no one may connect to or open a public sewer without first obtaining a permit, and the work has to be done by a plumber the owner employs who is licensed as a master plumber by the State of New Jersey. The authorized plumber must also post security — the code calls for a bond or deposit and holds the plumber responsible for the site for six months before the work is finally approved. For a Newark owner, that means the first call is to a licensed master plumber who knows the city's permit and bond process, not to an unlicensed digger.

Keeping Groundwater Out of an Overburdened System

Every gallon of clean water that leaks into a Newark lateral has somewhere worse to go: into a combined system that already discharges through 17 outfalls when it rains. Groundwater slips in through separated joints, roots pry the pipe open wider each season, and the extra flow is what the city's netting facilities and overflow program are fighting downstream. A homeowner who seals a leaking service line is doing the same job at the parcel that the city does at the outfall — taking clean water out of a pipe that was never meant to carry it, and easing the wet-weather surge that drives an overflow to the Passaic.

Trenchless Lining in Newark's Paved Core

Cured-in-place lining rebuilds a lateral in place. A felt tube saturated with resin is inverted into the old pipe and cured hard — by steam, hot water, or ultraviolet light — into a jointless pipe-within-a-pipe that grips the host and closes the cracks and root paths water was using. On Newark's tightly paved blocks that is often the only sensible route: instead of cutting a trench through a city street or sidewalk and restoring it afterward, a licensed plumber reaches the run through one access point and cures the liner in hours. The pipe already in the ground is renewed rather than dug out, and the infiltration the combined system can least afford is shut off.

The Newark Lines a Liner Can't Save

Lining depends on a host pipe that still holds its shape. Where a Newark lateral has been crushed flat, torn apart at an offset break, or has slumped into a dip that pools sewage, the liner may not seat or set, and a run a root mass has already shattered can be too far gone to reline. The honest move then is to burst the old pipe and draw a new one along its path, or to open-cut the failed length. A licensed master plumber runs the camera first and shows the footage; if a contractor pitches a liner without scoping the pipe, that is a reason to get the inspection before agreeing to anything.

Old Housing Over an Aging System

Newark's roughly 121,600 housing units span a century and a half of building, and it is the pre-war share that matters underground: close to a quarter of the stock went up before 1940, and more than four in ten before 1960, with the typical unit dating to the 1960s. The clay, brick, and early cast-iron laterals laid alongside that housing have spent decades cracking and pulling apart at the joints. Those are the runs quietly feeding groundwater into the combined system the city is working to control, and because they are structurally intact but leaking, they tend to be exactly the pipes a liner can renew without a full dig.
faq: Who pays for a sewer lateral repair in Newark?

The property owner. Under Newark's Title 32, the city's Division of Sewers and Water Supply builds and repairs the portion of the building sewer beyond the curbline, but the code states this is done at the owner's expense, so the lateral is the owner's financial responsibility.
Do I need a licensed contractor to work on a Newark sewer line?

Yes. No one may connect to or open a public sewer without a permit, and the work must be done by a plumber licensed as a master plumber by the State of New Jersey, who must post a bond and remains responsible for the site for six months before final approval.
Does Newark have combined sewers?

Yes. About eleven square miles of Newark are served by a combined sewer system with 17 permitted overflow outfalls — twelve along the Passaic River and five around the Newark Liberty Airport peripheral ditch — and the city runs eleven netting facilities to capture floatables.
Is CIPP lining allowed for a Newark lateral?

Trenchless rehabilitation of an existing lateral is a recognized repair, but it must still be done by a licensed master plumber under a city permit. Use a plumber who cameras the line first and handles Newark's permit and bond requirements.
Why does sealing infiltration matter in Newark?

Because Newark has combined sewers, groundwater leaking into private laterals adds to wet-weather flow that overflows at the city's 17 outfalls. Lining a cracked lateral keeps that clean water out of the system the city is under permit to control.

Paterson.metaTitle: Paterson, NJ Sewer Lateral Rules & CIPP Lining
Paterson.metaDescription: Unusual for New Jersey, Paterson repairs the curb-to-main sewer lateral at no cost to owners, who own the house connection. See the split rules and where CIPP lining fits.
Paterson.article:
Paterson Splits the Lateral in a Way Most Cities Don't

Paterson's sewer rules are worth reading carefully, because the city divides responsibility differently from almost every other place in New Jersey. Under Chapter 407, the code defines two separate segments. The "sewer lateral" runs from the curbline out to the main, and the "house connection" runs from the curbline into the building. What surprises most owners is that the city repairs the sewer lateral — the curb-to-main portion — at no cost to the property owner. The owner's responsibility is the house connection from the curb to the building, plus keeping the entire run clean. Knowing which segment is failing changes who pays for the fix.

What the Owner Owns, and What the City Covers

The practical breakdown is this: if the problem is between the curb and the main in the street, that is the city's repair under Chapter 407. If it is between the curb and your building, it is yours, and you install a new house connection at your own cost, with narrow exceptions the Council can grant in redevelopment or affordable-housing areas. The code also puts cleaning and rodding of the whole connection on the owner. So before commissioning any repair in Paterson, the first step is a camera inspection to establish exactly where the defect sits relative to the curb — it determines the bill.

Permits, the City Engineer, and Opening a Street

Sewer-connection work in Paterson runs through the code's permit process: an application, city investigation and approval, permit issuance, and inspection, with the City Engineer reviewing plans. Opening a street to reach the line is a separate matter under Chapter 435, which forbids any excavation in a street without a permit from the city, requires liability insurance and a performance bond covering the full restoration cost, and mandates repaving to state specification. For a homeowner that means a legitimate Paterson sewer repair is permitted, insured, bonded, and inspected — a reason to hire a contractor who already works within that framework. Because the responsibility hinges on which side of the curb a defect sits, most Paterson jobs sensibly start with that camera inspection before a permit is even pulled.

Why Infiltration Still Matters on the Owner's Side

Even though Paterson repairs the curb-to-main sewer lateral itself, the owner's house connection is still a live source of clean-water intrusion. Groundwater works in through cracked joints and roots widen the openings, and since every one of the city's overflow outfalls empties into the Passaic River, that extra flow lands in a single, hard-worked receiving water. The city built a facility to strain debris out of those combined-sewer discharges, but the cheapest gallon to treat is the one that never enters the pipe. Sealing the building-to-curb connection you are responsible for keeps groundwater out of the system before it ever reaches an outfall on the Passaic.

Lining the House Connection Without a Trench

For the owner's segment, cured-in-place lining is hard to beat. An epoxy-impregnated sleeve is winched into the existing house connection and hardened into a smooth inner wall, bridging the fractured joints and root gaps that let groundwater in. Because Paterson is dense and heavily paved, the appeal is avoiding a dig: the sleeve goes in through a compact pit and cures within a day, sparing the yard, the driveway, or the older street above it. It restores the curb-to-building run the owner is on the hook for while cutting the infiltration that feeds the city's overflows — a repair matched to exactly the part of the line that is yours.

When the House Connection Needs Replacing

A sleeve still needs a pipe worth relining. A Paterson house connection that has caved in, twisted out of round, or dropped into a belly that holds water may refuse the liner or fail to hold it, and a length a heavy root mass has broken apart may need replacing outright. There the sturdier answer is pipe bursting, which pulls a new pipe through the old route, or an open excavation. A dependable contractor proves the pipe's state on video before recommending a method, and steers the owner to replacement when the footage calls for it rather than lining a connection that cannot carry a liner.

Mill-Era Housing and Its House Connections

Paterson grew up as a mill city, and its house connections carry that age. About a third of its 52,500 or so units were built before 1940, and roughly three in five before 1960, with the median home landing in the 1950s. The connections that came with all that dense, older construction have had generations to fracture at the joints and let roots probe in. On the curb-to-building segment the owner is responsible for, those are the lines most apt to be leaking toward the Passaic — and, because the pipe is usually cracked rather than gone, good candidates to reline rather than trench out.
faq: Who repairs the sewer lateral in Paterson?

It depends on the segment. Under Chapter 407, the city repairs the 'sewer lateral' from the curbline to the main at no cost to the owner, while the property owner is responsible for the 'house connection' from the curbline into the building, plus cleaning the entire run.
How do I know which part of my Paterson sewer line is my responsibility?

By where the defect sits relative to the curb. A problem between the curb and the main in the street is the city's repair; a problem between the curb and your building is yours. A camera inspection is the way to establish which segment has failed before any work is commissioned.
What permits are needed for sewer work in Paterson?

Sewer-connection work runs through the code's permit process with City Engineer review, and opening a street requires a separate permit under Chapter 435, with liability insurance, a performance bond covering restoration, and repaving to specification.
Is CIPP lining a good option for a Paterson house connection?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions in the owner's curb-to-building house connection without a full excavation, reducing the infiltration that adds to the combined-sewer flow reaching the Passaic River.
Does Paterson have combined sewers?

Yes. Paterson is a combined-sewer city and all of its permitted overflow outfalls discharge to the Passaic River. The city has invested in controlling those discharges, including a facility to strain debris from combined-sewer overflows.

Elizabeth.metaTitle: Elizabeth, NJ Sewer Rules, CSOs & CIPP Lining
Elizabeth.metaDescription: Elizabeth carries 29 combined sewer overflow outfalls, most to the Elizabeth River, with treatment by the Joint Meeting in the city itself. See the rules and where CIPP lining fits.
Elizabeth.article:
Twenty-Nine Outfalls and a Regional Plant in the City

Elizabeth carries one of the heaviest combined-sewer burdens of any New Jersey city. Under its NJDEP combined-sewer permit, the city has 29 active overflow outfalls, and 20 of them discharge to the Elizabeth River — the single most CSO-burdened receiving water among the state's northern cities — with the rest going to the Arthur Kill, Newark Bay, and the Elizabeth Channel. Unlike Newark and Paterson, whose flow goes to the Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission, Elizabeth's wastewater is treated by the Joint Meeting of Essex and Union Counties at a regional plant located within Elizabeth itself, discharging to the Arthur Kill.

Who Is Responsible for the Sewer Connection

As in the rest of New Jersey, the service connection from an Elizabeth building to the public main is generally the property owner's to maintain, and the everyday cost of a cracked or root-blocked lateral falls on the owner rather than the city. Elizabeth's detailed sewer rules live in its municipal code under Public Services, and the exact chapter and section governing lateral ownership and permits are best confirmed with the city's engineering or sewer office before work begins. The safe assumption for a homeowner is that the lateral is theirs to repair, and the first step is to confirm the specifics with the city.

Permits and Opening the Street

Connecting to or working on Elizabeth's public sewer requires a city permit, and reaching the line under a public street brings in the city's street-opening rules, which typically call for insurance, a restoration bond, and inspection before the trench is closed. Because those requirements sit in the municipal code that the city administers directly, an Elizabeth owner should have the contractor confirm the current permit, bond, and inspection requirements with the city engineer's office — a permitted, inspected job is the norm, and an unpermitted dig into a city sewer can be ordered reopened. Because Elizabeth administers its code directly and its online ordinance can be hard to search, calling the city engineer's office before the work is the surest way to learn the current fees, bond amounts, and inspection steps, and to confirm which office signs off on the connection itself.

Cutting Infiltration Into a Heavily Loaded System

With 29 outfalls, Elizabeth's combined system has little slack in a storm, and most of that overflow reaches a single stressed waterway, the Elizabeth River. Nearly every outfall now carries solids-and-floatables controls, but those screen the discharge — they do not shrink the wet-weather volume that causes it. That volume is where a private lateral comes in: groundwater seeping through cracked joints and roots adds directly to it. Sealing a leaking service line removes that infiltration at the source, which is precisely the reduction the city's long-term control effort is chasing across the whole combined district.

Trenchless Repair in Elizabeth's Tight Blocks

Cured-in-place lining suits Elizabeth's dense, older streets. A resin-impregnated liner is drawn into the existing service pipe and cured into a continuous new wall inside it, closing the cracks and root openings that admit groundwater. Rather than trench across a narrow block and restore the pavement, the work is done through a small access pit and finished in a day, leaving the surface intact. It renews the pipe already buried and takes infiltration out of a system that overflows to the Elizabeth River — a low-disruption repair for an owner responsible for the lateral and a clean-water gain for a city carrying 29 outfalls.

Where an Elizabeth Liner Reaches Its Limit

Not every Elizabeth lateral can be lined. A pipe that has collapsed, gone badly out of round, or settled into a low run that ponds water may not take a liner or keep its form once cured, and a service a root mass has fractured into pieces can be past saving. The durable choice then is bursting the old pipe to pull a new one through, or excavating the failed section. A reliable contractor scopes the run on camera, shows the owner what is there, and points to replacement when the footage demands it — never selling a liner for a pipe the camera shows cannot hold one.

Aging Stock Behind 29 Outfalls

Elizabeth's housing sits behind one of the heaviest overflow burdens in the state. Of its roughly 48,900 units, better than a quarter predate 1940 and more than half predate 1960, the median unit dating to the 1950s. Service lines set with that housing have had decades to open at the joints, and the districts holding the oldest homes tend to sit above the outfalls carrying the most flow to the Elizabeth River. Sealing one of those cracked-but-standing laterals with a liner takes a household's groundwater out of a system already discharging through 29 outfalls — a small contribution to the same reduction the long-term plan is chasing.
faq: Who is responsible for a sewer lateral in Elizabeth?

Generally the property owner. As across New Jersey, the service connection from your building to the public main is the owner's to maintain, and the cost of a cracked or blocked lateral falls on the owner. Confirm the exact ordinance section and permit rules with the city before starting work.
How many combined sewer overflow outfalls does Elizabeth have?

Under its NJDEP combined-sewer permit, Elizabeth has 29 active CSO outfalls, and 20 of them discharge to the Elizabeth River, with the rest to the Arthur Kill, Newark Bay, and the Elizabeth Channel. Nearly all have solids-and-floatables controls installed.
Who treats Elizabeth's wastewater?

The Joint Meeting of Essex and Union Counties, at a regional treatment plant located within Elizabeth itself, which discharges to the Arthur Kill — unlike Newark and Paterson, whose flow goes to the Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission.
Is CIPP lining a good fit for an Elizabeth lateral?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions in an old lateral without a full excavation, reducing the infiltration that adds to the combined-sewer flow discharging to the Elizabeth River.
Do I need a permit for sewer work in Elizabeth?

Yes. Connecting to or working on the public sewer requires a city permit, and opening a public street brings in the city's street-opening rules — insurance, a restoration bond, and inspection. Confirm the current requirements with the city engineer's office.

Jersey City.metaTitle: Jersey City, NJ Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining
Jersey City.metaDescription: Jersey City's JCMUA pumps wastewater under the Hackensack to be treated, owns 21 CSO outfalls, and puts the lateral on owners. See the rules and where CIPP lining fits.
Jersey City.article:
A System That Pumps Its Sewage Under a River

Jersey City's water and sewer systems are run by the Jersey City Municipal Utilities Authority, and its wastewater takes an unusual route: the JCMUA converted its old treatment plants to pumping stations and now sends the city's sewage under the Hackensack River to the Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission's Newark Bay plant. Much of the city is served by a combined sewer system that carries sewage and stormwater together, with 21 combined-sewer overflow discharge points that release to the harbor and river in heavy rain. That combined-sewer setup, and the regional long-term control plan Jersey City takes part in, frame every private lateral repair in the city.

The Lateral Belongs to the Property Owner

The JCMUA's sewer rules put the service lateral on the owner: it is owned by the property owner from the sewer main to the building. That is a cleaner rule than the split-responsibility codes some New Jersey cities use — in Jersey City the whole run from the main to your building is yours to maintain and repair. The rules also require that where an existing lateral is reused, it be cleaned and televised, with an inspection report from a New Jersey licensed plumber, so the authority expects the pipe's condition to be documented before it is put back into service.

Permits, Inspection, and Opening a Road

Sewer-connection permits in Jersey City are issued by the JCMUA under its rules and regulations, which also govern road and street openings and require inspection during construction. For a homeowner, that means the work is a permitted, inspected job from the start, and the licensed plumber's camera report is part of the process rather than an optional extra. Hiring a contractor who already works within the JCMUA's permit and inspection framework — and who can produce the required televised inspection — is the way to keep a lateral repair moving without a stop-work surprise. The JCMUA's own application forms and inspection schedule govern the timing, so a contractor who files early and books the required inspection keeps a Jersey City lateral job from stalling between the pit being dug and the connection being signed off.

The Required Camera Report Works in a Liner's Favor

Jersey City's rules already push toward a sound lateral: a reused line has to be cleaned and televised, with a report from a licensed plumber, before it goes back into service. That camera work is exactly where a good lining job begins, so the authority's inspection requirement and a trenchless repair pull in the same direction. It matters here because the city's flow is pumped under the Hackensack to be treated, and groundwater leaking into a lateral adds to the wet-weather volume discharging through 21 overflow points. Sealing that intrusion trims the load the system pumps and the overflow the regional plan is working to cut.

Lining Fits a Dense, Pumped System

Cured-in-place lining is well matched to Jersey City's crowded blocks. A resin liner is pulled into the existing lateral and cured into a seamless pipe bonded to the host, sealing the cracks and root paths that let groundwater in. Rather than open a trench in a narrow street or a historic-district sidewalk, the run is lined through one compact access point and cured within a day — and the televised inspection the authority requires doubles as the pre-lining scope. The pipe already in the ground is renewed instead of torn out, keeping clean water out of a system that has to pump everything under the river to the plant.

When Jersey City Pipe Is Past Lining

A liner still needs a pipe worth keeping. A Jersey City lateral that has crushed flat, sheared at an offset, or bowed into a dip that traps flow may not accept a liner or hold it once cured, and a run roots have splintered can be too degraded to reline. There the sound repair is pipe bursting or an open cut, and because the authority requires the televised inspection anyway, the footage settles it — a reputable plumber will read the camera and recommend replacement when the pipe cannot support a liner, rather than lining it regardless.

A Housing Mix of Brownstones and New Towers

Few cities show Jersey City's spread of building ages. Among roughly 132,600 units, close to three in ten predate 1940 while nearly the same share have gone up since 2000 — brownstone blocks and waterfront towers in the same city — with the median unit around the 1960s. It is the pre-war housing, clustered in the historic neighborhoods, that holds the laterals most likely to be admitting groundwater into the combined system. Since the authority already wants those lines cleaned and televised, a cracked older lateral is often best renewed with a liner while the camera is down it, rather than opened up in a tightly built block.
faq: Who owns the sewer lateral in Jersey City?

The property owner. The Jersey City Municipal Utilities Authority's sewer rules state the lateral is owned by the property owner from the sewer main to the building, so the entire run is the owner's to maintain and repair.
Does Jersey City require an inspection of my sewer lateral?

Yes. The JCMUA rules require that a reused existing lateral be cleaned and televised, with an inspection report from a New Jersey licensed plumber, so the pipe's condition must be documented before it is put back into service.
Where does Jersey City's wastewater go?

The JCMUA converted its treatment plants to pumping stations and sends the city's sewage under the Hackensack River to the Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission's Newark Bay plant. The city has a combined sewer system with 21 overflow discharge points.
Is CIPP lining a good fit in Jersey City?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions in an old lateral without a full excavation, and the televised camera inspection the JCMUA requires is the same work a quality liner job begins with.
Does Jersey City have combined sewers?

Yes. Much of Jersey City is served by a combined sewer system with 21 combined-sewer overflow discharge points, and the city participates in a regional long-term control plan to reduce those overflows.

Camden.metaTitle: Camden, NJ Sewer Rules, CSOs & CIPP Lining
Camden.metaDescription: Camden owners maintain the sewer service to the curb, the county authority treats the flow, and rain gardens fight ~70 overflow events a year. See the rules and where CIPP fits.
Camden.article:
Three Owners, One Combined System, Seventy Overflows a Year

Camden's combined sewer system is shared: the City of Camden, neighboring Gloucester City, and the Camden County Municipal Utilities Authority each own portions of it, with the CCMUA providing regional treatment at its Delaware River facility. The system is old and overloaded — in an average year the Camden area experiences roughly 70 combined-sewer overflow events, far above the handful the EPA holds up as a target. That scale is why the City, Gloucester City, and CCMUA jointly built a long-term control plan aimed at capturing and treating about 85 percent of the combined sewage generated in a typical year, and it frames every private lateral repair in the city.

The Owner Maintains the Service to the Curb

Camden splits lateral responsibility at the curb. Under the city code, the property owner must keep and maintain the service pipes from the house connection to the curb, while the city maintains the street side of the curbline; separately, every property owner making a sewer connection does so at their own cost and expense. So the segment from your building to the curb is yours to keep in repair, and the everyday cost of a cracked or root-blocked service on that side lands on the owner — a good reason to understand where the curb line falls before a repair is needed.

Permits From the City, and Sometimes the County

Connecting to Camden's sewer requires a permit from the city under its plumbing standards, plus a street-opening permit from the city's capital-improvements division for work in the roadway; disconnecting a lateral requires a street-opening permit and a permit to disconnect at the main. The code also recognizes that the CCMUA may issue sewer-connection permits and set connection fees for new construction and rehabilitation. For a homeowner that means checking whether the city, the county authority, or both are involved before the work starts, and hiring a contractor who can navigate the right permit path. Because a Camden job can touch both a city plumbing permit and a county authority connection, confirming at the outset which office signs off on your specific work saves a return trip once the trench is already open.

Rain Gardens Above, Leaking Pipe Below

Camden's whole clean-water strategy is about volume: with roughly 70 overflow events in an average year, the city and county are installing rain gardens and green infrastructure through the Camden SMART Initiative to hold stormwater back from the combined sewers. A leaking private service works against that from below, letting groundwater into the sanitary pipe through cracked joints and root openings. Sealing the owner's building-to-curb segment does at the parcel what the rain gardens do at the street — it keeps clean water out of a combined system that overflows dozens of times a year and is under a plan to capture most of that flow.

Lining the Owner's Curb-to-Building Segment

For the segment Camden puts on the owner, a cured-in-place repair earns its keep. An installer works a resin-soaked sleeve into the service pipe and sets it firm, forming a seamless inner wall that spans the fractures and root openings where groundwater slips in. There is no need to open a trench across a yard, a driveway, or an older paved street — the sleeve enters through one pit and hardens on site. The buried pipe is brought back to a watertight state instead of being excavated, and the building-to-curb run the owner answers for is fixed while infiltration that would otherwise swell the overflows is turned away.

When a Camden Service Needs Replacing

A sleeve cannot revive a service that has given out. A Camden line that has been crushed, forced apart at a joint, or has slumped into a low pocket where waste collects will not hold a liner, and one a root mass has torn open may be beyond saving. Bursting the old pipe to draw a new one through, or a straight excavation, is the answer there, and a sound contractor lets the video make the case — calling for a replacement outright when the service cannot carry a liner rather than talking an owner into one.

Some of the State's Oldest Service Lines

Camden's housing is among the oldest in New Jersey, and its service pipes show every year of it. Nearly four in ten of its roughly 27,900 units date to before 1940, and close to two-thirds to before 1960, the median home sitting in the 1940s. Pipe laid with housing that old has cracked and separated at the joints over the decades, and the blocks with the oldest homes are the ones adding the most groundwater to a system that already overflows dozens of times a year. Where those owner-side lines are broken but not collapsed, relining is usually the least disruptive way to shut the infiltration off.
faq: Who is responsible for the sewer service line in Camden?

Responsibility splits at the curb. Under the city code, the property owner maintains the service pipes from the house connection to the curb, while the city maintains the street side of the curbline, and every owner making a sewer connection does so at their own cost.
Who treats Camden's wastewater?

The Camden County Municipal Utilities Authority (CCMUA) provides regional treatment at its Delaware River facility. The City of Camden, Gloucester City, and the CCMUA each own portions of the combined sewer system.
What is the Camden SMART Initiative?

Camden SMART is a green-infrastructure partnership of the City of Camden, the CCMUA, the state, Rutgers, and local organizations that installs rain gardens and other features to keep stormwater out of the combined sewers, reducing the roughly 70 overflow events the area sees in an average year.
Is CIPP lining a good option in Camden?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions in the owner's building-to-curb service pipe without a full excavation, cutting the infiltration that adds to the combined-sewer overflows the city is working to reduce.
Do I need a city or county permit for sewer work in Camden?

Possibly both. Connecting requires a city permit under its plumbing standards plus a street-opening permit for roadway work, and the CCMUA may issue sewer-connection permits and set fees for new construction and rehabilitation — so confirm the right permit path before starting.

Trenton.metaTitle: Trenton, NJ Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining
Trenton.metaDescription: Trenton collects and treats its own combined-sewer wastewater and runs its own water utility; owners repair the curb-to-building service. See the rules and where CIPP fits.
Trenton.article:
One City Government Runs Water, Sewers, and Treatment

Trenton is unusual among New Jersey's combined-sewer cities because it does everything itself. The Trenton Sewer Utility collects the city's wastewater and treats it at the city's own plant on the Delaware River, rather than sending it to a regional authority the way Jersey City and Camden do. The same city government also owns and runs Trenton Water Works, one of the oldest municipally owned water utilities in the state. So in Trenton a single public entity controls the water supply, the sewer collection system, and the wastewater treatment — a rare degree of local control that shapes how sewer work is permitted and inspected.

The Owner Repairs From the Curb to the Building

Trenton's code puts the service repair on the property owner: it is the owner's responsibility to make all necessary repairs to the service from the curbline to the building, and the owner excavates at their own expense. The code does soften that in one narrow way — a possible reimbursement of up to $250 if the problem turns out to originate between the curb and the street or main connection. But the working rule for a homeowner is that the curb-to-building service is yours to keep in repair, and the reimbursement is a limited exception rather than the norm.

Permits, Inspection, and a Written Plumber Approval

Trenton controls sewer work closely. No connection between the curbline and the sewer main may be laid, connected, or covered except under the supervision of and after inspection by the Division of Water and Sewers, with a connection permit fee set in the code, and no discharge is allowed before the Division approves and accepts the connection. On top of that, no plumber may extend or alter service pipes without a written permit from the Division. For an owner that means hiring a plumber who will pull the Division's permit and schedule the required inspection before the trench is closed. Since the Division both issues the permit and performs the inspection, a Trenton owner deals with a single city office from application through sign-off, which at least keeps the paperwork under one roof even when the repair itself is theirs to fund and to schedule around the required inspection.

Keeping Rain Out of a System the City Treats Itself

Because Trenton collects and treats its own combined-sewer flow, clean water leaking into the system is the city's cost twice over — once to convey it, once to treat it — and its green-infrastructure work is aimed squarely at keeping rainwater out of the sewers through trees, rain gardens, and rainwater capture. On a private service the same clean water enters through cracked joints and root paths as groundwater, and it ends up in the flow the city sends to the Delaware. Sealing the owner's curb-to-building segment removes that infiltration at the parcel, easing both the conveyance and the treatment the city handles.

Lining the Curb-to-Building Service

Cured-in-place lining fits the owner's segment in Trenton. A resin-saturated liner is pulled into the existing service and cured into a smooth, jointless pipe inside it, sealing the cracks and root openings that admit groundwater. Rather than cut a trench across the older streets and tight lots that fill the capital, the run is lined through a compact access point and finished in a day. It renews the curb-to-building pipe the owner is responsible for and cuts the infiltration that would otherwise add to the combined-sewer flow the city treats before discharging to the Delaware River.

When a Trenton Liner Won't Hold

A liner still needs a pipe that can hold it. A Trenton service that has collapsed, deformed out of round, or bellied into a run that ponds water may not seat a liner or keep it once cured, and a length roots have splintered may need replacement. There the sturdier repair is pipe bursting or an open cut, and since the Division of Water and Sewers inspects the work regardless, the camera decides it — a reliable plumber will read the footage and recommend replacement when the pipe cannot carry a liner, instead of lining it anyway.

The Oldest Housing of the Big Combined-Sewer Cities

Among New Jersey's large combined-sewer cities, Trenton's housing is the oldest of all. More than four in ten of its roughly 35,900 units predate 1940, and close to two-thirds predate 1960, with the median unit in the 1940s. The service lines that came with that housing have had the better part of a century to fracture and let roots in, and the capital's oldest neighborhoods are the ones contributing most to a combined system the city both conveys and treats. On the curb-to-building run the owner owns, a cracked-but-intact line is frequently a strong candidate for a liner rather than a full replacement.
faq: Who repairs the sewer service in Trenton?

The property owner. Trenton's code makes it the owner's responsibility to repair the service from the curbline to the building, at the owner's expense, with a possible reimbursement of up to $250 if the problem originates between the curb and the street or main connection.
Does Trenton treat its own wastewater?

Yes. Unlike Jersey City and Camden, the Trenton Sewer Utility collects and treats the city's wastewater at its own plant on the Delaware River, and the same city government also runs Trenton Water Works, one of the oldest municipal water utilities in the state.
What permits do I need for sewer work in Trenton?

A connection between the curbline and the main may only be made under the supervision of and after inspection by the Division of Water and Sewers, with a connection permit fee, and no plumber may extend or alter service pipes without a written permit from the Division.
Is CIPP lining a good option in Trenton?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions in the owner's curb-to-building service without a full excavation, reducing the infiltration that adds to the city's combined-sewer flow to the Delaware River.
Why does keeping rainwater out of the sewer matter in Trenton?

Because Trenton has a combined system that overflows to the Delaware in heavy rain. The city's green-infrastructure program aims to keep rainwater out of the sewers, and sealing a leaking private service removes infiltration at the property scale.

Atlantic City.metaTitle: Atlantic City, NJ Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining
Atlantic City.metaDescription: Atlantic City's sewers are run by a private BPU-regulated company on a barrier island with a high water table that pushes groundwater into cracked pipe. See the rules and where CIPP fits.
Atlantic City.article:
A Private Sewer Company on a Barrier Island

Atlantic City is different from almost every other New Jersey city in who runs its sewers. Water service comes from the Atlantic City Municipal Utilities Authority, but the sanitary collection system is owned and operated by the Atlantic City Sewerage Company, an investor-owned public utility regulated by the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities and in business since 1888. The company does not treat the sewage; it purchases treatment from the Atlantic County Utilities Authority, whose regional plant discharges to the Atlantic Ocean through an outfall. That private, BPU-regulated structure sets the rules for laterals here through a tariff rather than a municipal ordinance.

Where the Tariff Draws the Line

Because the sewer utility is a private company, lateral responsibility is set in its BPU-approved tariff rather than a city code. The split runs at the curb: the company owns and maintains the lateral from its mains to the curb, and the property owner is responsible from the curb box into and on the premises. So the segment from your building to the curb box is yours, and questions about it go to the sewerage company, not a municipal sewer office. For a homeowner that is an important distinction — the "utility" you deal with for a lateral in Atlantic City is a regulated private business.

Permits: the Company for the Sewer, the City for the Street

Connecting to the sanitary system runs through the Atlantic City Sewerage Company's own application and tariff process, not a municipal permit desk. Opening a street to reach the line is a separate city matter: Atlantic City's code requires a street-opening permit issued by the City Engineer, with a performance guaranty, a maintenance bond, liability insurance, and prompt pavement restoration. So a lateral repair here typically means coordinating the sewerage company's connection approval with a city street-opening permit — a good reason to hire a contractor familiar with both tracks. Coordinating the sewerage company's connection approval with the city's street-opening permit is the step owners most often overlook, and getting both lined up before the crew arrives avoids a stalled dig on a busy resort street.

A High Water Table That Feeds the Sanitary Lines

Atlantic City's barrier-island setting turns infiltration into a defining problem. Street elevations are low and the water table is high, so much of the island's sanitary pipe sits in saturated, tidal ground; the sewerage company runs seven pump stations to lift the flow off the island through force mains to the county plant. A cracked or root-opened lateral in that setting takes on groundwater readily, and every gallon of it is then pumped and treated needlessly. On a separated sanitary system, keeping the water table out of the pipe is the whole point — and the pressure to do so is greater here than almost anywhere else in the state.

Lining Against the Island's Groundwater

On saturated island ground, cured-in-place lining has a clear edge. A resin-impregnated liner is drawn into the existing lateral and cured into a continuous, watertight pipe inside it, closing the joints and root gaps the high water table exploits. Open trenching in sandy, tidal soil is its own problem — the walls want to slump and the hole wants to flood — so a liner installed through one compact access point, cured in a day, avoids that entirely. It renews the pipe already in place and shuts off the very defects that let the water table into the sanitary system the company pumps off the island.

When an Atlantic City Liner Won't Work

A liner still needs a pipe worth saving, even here. An Atlantic City lateral that has crushed flat, sheared at a break, or dropped into a belly that traps water may not take a liner or hold it once cured, and a run roots have broken apart may be past relining. There pipe bursting or an open cut is the more durable repair — though excavation in tidal ground is exacting — and a reliable contractor will camera the line, show the owner the footage, and recommend replacement when the pipe demands it. In saturated soil especially, a liner offered without an inspection first is a reason to require one.

Resort-Era Housing in Saturated Ground

Atlantic City's roughly 20,100 units mix older resort-era buildings with later construction: about a third predate 1940 and nearly half predate 1960, the median unit around the 1960s. What makes the age tell here is the ground it sits in — laterals from the older stock have been shifting and cracking in saturated island soil for decades, and those are the very lines the high water table exploits. A cracked but standing lateral in that setting is both the biggest infiltration risk and, because trenching in tidal sand is so difficult, one of the strongest cases for renewing the pipe with a liner instead of digging it out.
faq: Who runs the sewers in Atlantic City?

The sanitary collection system is owned and operated by the Atlantic City Sewerage Company, an investor-owned utility regulated by the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities since 1888. Water comes from the ACMUA, and treatment is purchased from the Atlantic County Utilities Authority, which discharges to the ocean.
Who is responsible for the sewer lateral in Atlantic City?

Responsibility splits at the curb under the sewerage company's BPU-approved tariff: the company maintains the lateral from its mains to the curb, and the property owner is responsible from the curb box into and on the premises.
Does Atlantic City have combined sewers?

No. Atlantic City runs a separate sanitary system plus a separate storm sewer system, and it is not a combined-sewer overflow community. Its main wet-weather concern is infiltration into sanitary lines, driven by a very high water table.
Is CIPP lining a good fit in Atlantic City?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions that let groundwater into a lateral — especially valuable on a barrier island with a high water table — and avoids trenching in sandy, tidal ground that tends to collapse and flood.
What permits do I need for sewer work in Atlantic City?

Connecting to the sanitary system runs through the Atlantic City Sewerage Company's application process, and opening a street requires a separate city street-opening permit from the City Engineer, with a bond, insurance, and pavement restoration.

East Orange.metaTitle: East Orange, NJ Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining
East Orange.metaDescription: In East Orange one municipal commission runs water and sewer, owners own the whole lateral, and a master plumber is required. See the rules and where CIPP lining fits.
East Orange.article:
One Municipal Commission for Water and Sewer

East Orange runs its utilities through an unusual local institution: the East Orange Water Commission, a municipally owned utility created by referendum in 1909 that provides both water and wastewater service and issues the city's sewer-connection permits. The city owns its own water supply — well fields in the roughly 2,300-acre East Orange Water Reserve, drawing the Passaic aquifer — and the same commission that manages that off-site reserve administers sewer connections back in the city. East Orange's sewage flows to a regional plant run by the Joint Meeting of Essex and Union Counties, which discharges to the Arthur Kill; the city itself runs a separated sanitary system, not a combined one.

The Whole Lateral Belongs to the Owner

East Orange keeps its lateral rule simple: under the city code, the property owner owns and maintains the lateral from the public-sewer trunk line to the building, and the cost and maintenance are the obligation of the abutting property owner. There is no split at the curb — the whole length is yours. A blocked or broken service is therefore a private matter from the trunk line to the building, which puts a premium on spotting a failing pipe early — ideally on camera — rather than meeting the problem as a backup during a storm.

A Master Plumber, a Permit, and a Street-Opening Permit

East Orange requires a sewer-connection permit, filed with and approved by the Executive Director of the Water Commission, with a $150 inspection fee and 48 hours' notice before inspection. The work has to be done under the direct supervision of a state-licensed master plumber — the code allows only a single-family homeowner to work on his own dwelling as an exception. Opening a street to reach the line brings in a separate excavation permit from the Director of Public Works, with liability insurance, deposits or a surety bond, and full pavement restoration. For a homeowner, that means a licensed master plumber and two permit tracks. Between the Water Commission's connection permit and the Public Works street-opening permit, an East Orange job typically runs through two municipal offices, so a plumber who lines both up in advance keeps the schedule from slipping once the crew is on site.

A Separated System Built to Exclude Clean Water

East Orange runs a separated sanitary system tributary to the regional plant, so its wet-weather worry is not an overflow but inflow and infiltration — clean water sneaking into pipes meant only for sewage. The code keeps sanitary and storm sewers apart and bars stormwater from the sanitary side, and on a private lateral the same intrusion arrives as groundwater through cracked joints and as roots that widen them. All of it becomes flow the regional plant must treat. Sealing a leaking lateral keeps that clean water out of the sanitary system, doing exactly what a separated system is designed to accomplish.

Lining the Full Owner-Owned Lateral

Since East Orange assigns the entire lateral to the owner, a single lining run can put the whole thing right. A master plumber saturates a tube with resin, pulls it from near the trunk main to the building, and sets it into one continuous barrier that closes the leaking joints and root intrusions along its length. The excavation is skipped — a lone entry point does the job, and service is back the same afternoon. A corroded, groundwater-drawing pipe becomes a sealed one without the lawn or pavement being touched, discharging the owner's full obligation in one visit and holding clean water clear of the plant-bound flow.

When an East Orange Liner Falls Short

Some East Orange laterals are simply too far gone. One that has flattened under load, lost its round profile, or dips where water stands will resist a liner or slump as it cures, and a pipe roots have pried open may need swapping out. The remedy is then a pull-through burst or a targeted dig, chosen only after a master plumber scopes the run and shows what the camera found. A liner is never the right sale for a pipe the footage proves cannot support one, and a straight recommendation to replace it is the honest outcome.

Dense Older Housing Over Tributary Pipe

East Orange's building stock leans old and dense. Of roughly 29,900 units, about three in ten predate 1940 and more than half predate 1960, the median unit dating to the 1950s. Much of it is apartment and two-family construction, and the laterals set beneath it have had decades to crack and admit roots. In a separated system tributary to the regional plant, each of those leaks becomes groundwater the plant has to treat, and the oldest neighborhoods carry the lines doing the most of it. Renewing a cracked-but-sound lateral with a liner is often the tidiest fix on a crowded lot.
faq: Who is responsible for the sewer lateral in East Orange?

The property owner. Under the city code, the owner owns and maintains the lateral from the public-sewer trunk line to the building, and the cost and maintenance are the obligation of the abutting property owner — there is no split at the curb.
Do I need a licensed plumber to work on my East Orange sewer line?

Yes. Plumbing and drainage work must be done under the direct supervision of a state-licensed master plumber, except that a single-family homeowner may work on his own dwelling. A sewer-connection permit from the Water Commission and a street-opening permit are also required.
Who runs water and sewer in East Orange?

The East Orange Water Commission, a municipally owned utility created by referendum in 1909, provides both water and wastewater service and issues sewer-connection permits. The city's sewage is treated regionally by the Joint Meeting of Essex and Union Counties.
Does East Orange have combined sewers?

No. East Orange runs a separated sanitary system tributary to the regional plant, so its wet-weather concern is inflow and infiltration into sanitary lines rather than combined-sewer overflows, and the code bars stormwater from the sanitary system.
Is CIPP lining a good fit in East Orange?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions that let groundwater into an old lateral without a full excavation, keeping infiltration out of the separated sanitary system the regional plant treats.

Edison.metaTitle: Edison, NJ Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining
Edison.metaDescription: Edison Township splits the lateral at the property line, treats its flow regionally through MCUA, and bans downspout connections. See the sewer rules and where CIPP lining fits.
Edison.article:
A Suburban Township on a Regional System

Edison is a large Middlesex County township that owns and runs its own sanitary sewer collection system through its Department of Water and Sewer, but sends the wastewater to be treated regionally by the Middlesex County Utilities Authority, which discharges to the Raritan River and Bay. Edison is one of roughly three dozen MCUA member municipalities, so it handles collection while treatment is a county-scale operation. Its system is a separated sanitary one — sewage and stormwater run in different pipes — which means Edison is not a combined-sewer overflow community, and its wet-weather concern is keeping clean water out of the sanitary lines.

The Lateral Splits at the Property Line

Edison's code draws the ownership line by pipe segment. It defines the "building public sewer lateral" — the utility-owned pipe from the main to the property line — separately from the "building sanitary sewer," which runs from the building to the property line and belongs to the owner. So the split is at the property line, not the curb: the township owns the in-street portion out to your property line, and you own the run from the building to that line. Knowing where the property line falls is what tells an Edison owner which part of a failing line is theirs to repair.

Connection Permits and Registered Contractors

Before connecting a building sewer to the service lateral, Edison requires a connection permit, and the excavation and plumbing work follow only once that permit is in hand. The code also requires contractors to register with the township's authorized agent before doing building-sewer or connection work, providing their name, address, and experience. That registration step is worth knowing in advance: an Edison sewer repair is expected to be done by a registered contractor under a connection permit, so the first move is to hire someone already set up to work in the township. Registering before the work and pulling the connection permit up front are the steps that keep an Edison job moving, since the township expects both to be in place before a crew breaks ground on the building sewer, and an unregistered contractor can be turned away at inspection even after the pipe is in.

Downspouts Out, and Groundwater Too

Edison's separated system works hard to keep clean water out of the sanitary sewer: the code bans rain conductors, downspouts, roof runoff, and stormwater inlets from connecting to it, classic inflow controls. Infiltration is the quieter version of the same problem — groundwater entering a private building sewer through cracked joints and root openings, then traveling to the county plant as flow that has to be treated. Sealing a leaking building sewer does for infiltration what the downspout ban does for inflow: it keeps rain and groundwater out of a pipe meant only for sewage, and out of the regional system Edison shares with dozens of other towns.

Lining Edison's Building-to-Property-Line Run

For the stretch Edison leaves to the owner, a trenchless repair is a tidy match. The installer works a resin tube into the building sewer and hardens it into a smooth, seamless pipe that bridges the split joints and root gaps letting groundwater through. On a suburban lot nothing gets trenched across the lawn or drive — the liner enters at a single point and sets within the day. It returns the buried pipe to a watertight condition and holds infiltration off the county system, a low-impact way to renew the owner's building-to-property-line pipe without tearing the property apart or pulling a road-opening permit.

When Edison Pipe Needs Replacing

Where an Edison building sewer has buckled, gone oval, or bellied into a low stretch, a liner can fail to seat or hold, and a section a root intrusion has broken apart usually calls for replacement. A pull-through burst or an open trench is the durable route in that case. A registered contractor should rest the recommendation on the camera pass, steering toward a fresh pipe whenever the footage rules a liner out — the point of scoping the line first is to avoid lining a run that was never going to keep it.

Postwar Suburban Housing and Its Pipe

Edison's housing runs younger than the state's old cities, and that shapes what is in the ground. The township holds around 42,700 units, much of it built during the postwar suburban boom of the mid-to-late twentieth century rather than before the war. Laterals of that vintage are not the century-old clay lines common in Newark or Trenton, but they are decades old all the same — old enough for joints to open and roots to find them. As Edison's mid-century service lines reach the age where infiltration starts, renewing a cracked one with a liner is usually the least disruptive option on a suburban property.
faq: Who owns the sewer lateral in Edison?

Ownership splits at the property line. Edison's code makes the township-owned 'building public sewer lateral' run from the main to the property line, while the owner's 'building sanitary sewer' runs from the building to the property line — so you own the run from your building to the property line.
Do I need a permit and a registered contractor in Edison?

Yes. A connection permit is required before excavation and plumbing to connect a building sewer, and contractors must register with the township's authorized agent — providing name, address, and experience — before doing building-sewer or connection work.
Does Edison have combined sewers?

No. Edison runs a separated sanitary system and is not a combined-sewer overflow community; its wastewater is treated regionally by the Middlesex County Utilities Authority. The code bars stormwater, roof runoff, and downspouts from the sanitary sewer.
Is CIPP lining a good fit in Edison?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions that let groundwater into a building sewer without a full excavation, keeping infiltration out of the separated sanitary system the county plant treats.
Can I connect my downspouts to the sewer in Edison?

No. Edison's code prohibits connecting rain conductors, downspouts, roof runoff, stormwater inlets, and groundwater to the sanitary sewer — standard inflow-and-infiltration controls for a separated system.

Clifton.metaTitle: Clifton, NJ Sewer Rules & CIPP Lining
Clifton.metaDescription: Clifton runs 159 miles of sanitary sewer separate from its storm drains, puts the whole lateral on owners, and treats through PVSC. See the rules and where CIPP lining fits.
Clifton.article:
A Separated System, Kept Deliberately Apart From the Storm Drains

Clifton's collection system is run by the City of Clifton Sewer Utility, a municipally owned utility whose day-to-day work is handled by the Public Works Sewer Division, and the wastewater is treated by the Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission. Clifton is a separated-sewer city: its Public Works figures show about 158.8 miles of sanitary sewer kept physically apart from roughly 50 miles of storm drains. That separation is the defining trait of the system, and it means Clifton is not a combined-sewer overflow community — its wet-weather concern is keeping stormwater and groundwater from leaking into the sanitary lines.

The Whole Lateral Is the Owner's

Clifton assigns the entire lateral to the property owner. Under the city code, each property owner must maintain and be responsible for the proper upkeep, repair, and replacement of the sewer lateral from the public right-of-way to the building. There is no split at the curb or the property line — the full run from the right-of-way to your building falls to you. Every foot of it is a private responsibility, which is a strong argument for scoping a suspect line early — before a slow drain becomes a backup and a planned repair becomes an emergency dig.

Connection Approval, Downspout Rules, and Opening a Street

Clifton requires municipal approval to connect to the sanitary sewer, with a connection fee, and it also requires approval — with an administrative fee — before any roof downspout, foundation drain, or areaway drain may be connected, part of the city's effort to keep inflow out of the sanitary system. Opening a street to reach the line is governed by a separate street-openings chapter: it is unlawful to excavate in a street without a permit from the City Engineer, with a surety bond and liability insurance required, though emergency sewer repairs are exempt from the fee while still needing a permit. Between the sewer utility's connection approval and the City Engineer's street-opening permit, a Clifton job usually clears two separate approvals, and confirming both before the crew arrives keeps the work from pausing once the access pit is already open, emergency sewer repairs being the one exception the code carves out.

A System Kept Apart, and Worth Keeping Tight

Clifton keeps its sanitary sewer physically separate from its storm drains — about 159 miles of one, 50 of the other — and even maintains the city's brooks and streams as a distinct network. The point of all that separation is to keep clean water out of the sewage pipes, so infiltration into a private lateral runs directly against the system's design. Groundwater enters through cracked joints and roots widen them, and the extra flow travels to the Passaic Valley plant for treatment. Sealing a leaking lateral upholds the separation the whole system is built on, keeping the sanitary line carrying only what it is meant to.

One Lining Pass for the Whole Lateral

Clifton's rule that the owner holds the run from the right-of-way in means a liner can address it in one continuous shot. The installer inverts a resin-soaked tube through the pipe and sets it hard, forming a jointless sleeve that spans every fracture and root gap between the street and the house. No trench crosses the lawn or roadway; the sleeve enters at a compact pit and cures in hours. The buried pipe is renewed rather than dug out, and because the entire lateral is the owner's, that one pass settles the whole responsibility while shutting groundwater out of the deliberately separated lines.

When a Clifton Liner Won't Hold

A Clifton lateral that has collapsed inward, twisted out of true, or settled into a pocket holding water can turn a liner away or deform it as it cures, and a run splintered by roots may have to be replaced. The stronger fix is bursting the line or cutting it open. A dependable contractor reads the video before anything else and calls for replacement when the pipe is past what a liner can rescue — refusing to line a failed pipe is the straight answer here, not a missed job.

Heavily Mid-Century Housing

Clifton's housing is unusually concentrated in the mid-twentieth century. Of roughly 34,100 units, about three in ten predate 1940, but a striking seven in ten predate 1960 — nearly half of everything went up between 1940 and 1969 — with the median unit in the 1950s. Laterals laid with that postwar wave are now decades into service and reaching the point where joints crack and roots intrude. Because Clifton makes the owner responsible for the whole run, those aging lines are private end to end, and where a line is cracked rather than collapsed, one lining pass from the right-of-way to the building is often the cleanest way to seal it.
faq: Who is responsible for the sewer lateral in Clifton?

The property owner, for the whole run. Under the city code, each owner must maintain and be responsible for the upkeep, repair, and replacement of the sewer lateral from the public right-of-way to the building — there is no split at the curb or property line.
Does Clifton have combined sewers?

No. Clifton is a separated-sewer city, with about 158.8 miles of sanitary sewer kept physically apart from roughly 50 miles of storm drains, so it is not a combined-sewer overflow community. Its concern is keeping stormwater and groundwater out of the sanitary lines.
Who treats Clifton's wastewater?
The Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission (PVSC). The collection system is run by the City of Clifton Sewer Utility, with day-to-day maintenance by the Public Works Sewer Division.
Can I connect a downspout or foundation drain to my Clifton sewer?

Only with municipal approval and an administrative fee. Clifton requires approval before any roof downspout, foundation drain, or areaway drain is connected, as part of keeping inflow out of the separated sanitary system.
Is CIPP lining a good fit in Clifton?

Often, yes. A cured-in-place liner seals the cracks and root intrusions that let groundwater into a lateral without a full excavation, and because the owner is responsible for the whole run, a single lining pass can address the entire lateral from right-of-way to building.
